title: How do climate and seasons affect daily life?
essentialQuestion: How do long-term climate patterns shape how people live and work?
learningGoal: Explain the difference between weather and climate, and describe one way people adapt to the seasons.

sections.heading: Weather and climate are different
sections.text: Weather is what the air is like at one time and place. It can be hot, cold, wet, dry or windy, and it can change in minutes. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over a long time. To describe a climate, scientists usually study at least 30 years of weather records. Look at Sunrise School. Heavy rain this afternoon is weather. The fact that the rainy season has been much wetter than the dry season for 30 years is climate. Here is a simple way to remember the difference: weather is what you get today, but climate is what you expect.
sections.simpler: Weather is what the air is like now. It can be hot or cold. It can be wet, dry or windy. Weather can change fast. Climate is the usual weather in a place. It is a pattern over many years. Scientists look at 30 years or more. At Sunrise School, heavy rain today is weather. A wet rainy season every year is climate. Weather is what you get today. Climate is what you expect.

sections.heading: Seasons follow a pattern
sections.text: A season is a part of the year with its own kind of weather. Far from the equator, many places have four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. These seasons happen because Earth is tilted as it travels around the Sun. Near the equator, it is warm all year, so the seasons are usually rainy or dry instead. In South Asia and Southeast Asia, a seasonal wind called the monsoon brings heavy rain for several months. In India, for example, most of the year's rain falls between June and September.
sections.simpler: A season is a part of the year. Each season has its own weather. Some places have four seasons. They are spring, summer, autumn and winter. Earth tips a little to one side as it goes around the Sun. This makes the seasons. The equator is a line around Earth's middle. Places near it are warm all year. There, seasons are wet or dry. In India, a wind called the monsoon brings rain. Most rain falls from June to September.

sections.heading: People adapt to climate and seasons
sections.text: People change how they live to suit their climate. These changes are called adaptations. In hot, dry places, such as parts of Mali and Yemen, many buildings have thick mud-brick walls that help keep rooms cool. In Mongolia, some herders move their animals between summer and winter camps. In many farming communities, people plant crops when the rainy season begins. Sunrise School adapts too. Covered walkways keep students dry, and water stations help on hot days. A good adaptation is based on evidence and works for everyone, including people who use wheelchairs.
sections.simpler: People change how they live to fit the climate. This is called adaptation. In some hot, dry places, homes have thick mud walls. The walls keep rooms cool. In Mongolia, some families move with their animals each season. Many farmers plant seeds when the rains start. Sunrise School adapts too. Covered paths keep students dry. Water stations help on hot days. A good adaptation helps everyone.

glossary.definition: What the air is like now: hot, cold, wet, dry or windy.
glossary.example: Heavy rain at Sunrise School this afternoon is weather.

glossary.definition: The usual weather in a place over many years.
glossary.example: The climate at Sunrise School has a wet season and a dry season.

glossary.definition: Something that happens again and again in the same way.
glossary.example: A wet rainy season every year is a pattern at Sunrise School.

glossary.definition: A part of the year with its own kind of weather.
glossary.example: At Sunrise School, the rainy season is much wetter than the dry season.

glossary.definition: A wind that brings heavy rain for months each year.
glossary.example: In India, the monsoon brings most of the year's rain.

glossary.definition: A change people make so they can live well with the conditions.
glossary.example: Covered walkways at Sunrise School are an adaptation to the rainy season.

checks.question: Which Sunrise School record tells you about climate?

options.text: The rainy season has been wet for 30 years.
options.feedback: Yes. Thirty years of records show a long pattern. That is climate.

options.text: Heavy rain delayed the walk home this afternoon.
options.feedback: Not quite. One afternoon of rain is weather. Look for a pattern over many years.

options.text: It rained on 18 days during this month.
options.feedback: Not quite. One month is still too short to show climate. Look for a pattern over many years.

checks.question: Which of these is an adaptation to hot days?

options.text: Writing down how hot it is each day
options.feedback: Not quite. Writing down how hot it is gives evidence, but it does not change anything. Look for a change that helps people.
Yes. Water stations are a change that helps students cope with hot days.
Not quite. Forgetting about the heat does not help anyone. Look for a change that helps people.

write.prompt: Choose one way Sunrise School could adapt to its climate, and use one fact from the records. Say how it would help all students, including students who use wheelchairs.
sentenceStarters: This is a fact about climate because...
selfCheck: I used one fact from the records.
I chose one way the school could adapt.
I explained how it helps all students.
write.example: The records show that the rainy season has been much wetter than the dry season for 30 years. This is a fact about climate because it is a long pattern. I recommend more covered walkways between the classrooms and the gate. This would help students because they could stay dry when it rains. It should also work for students who use wheelchairs. So the walkways need ramps, not only steps.

speak.partnerTask: Take turns. One person says an example, like 'It is windy today' or 'Summers here are usually hot.' The other person says if it is weather or climate.
speak.independentTask: Say 'Weather is... Climate is...' and give one example of each.

watch.title: Causes and Effects of Climate Change
watch.why: It shows how scientists explain changes in climate over many years, which builds on the difference between weather and climate.
watch.beforeQuestion: Can one very hot day prove that the climate is changing? Why or why not?
watch.afterQuestion: Why do scientists need weather records from many years to understand climate?
watch.summary: This video explains how Earth's climate is changing. Some gases in the air, like carbon dioxide, trap heat from the Sun. They work a bit like the glass walls of a greenhouse, which keep plants warm. People burn coal, oil and gas for energy. This adds more of these gases to the air, so Earth is getting warmer. The video says a warmer Earth changes weather patterns. Large areas of ice in Greenland and Antarctica are melting, and the sea is rising. Some places now get stronger storms and heavier rain. Other places get longer dry times. This can make it harder to grow food. The video ends with a hopeful idea. People can use power from the sun and wind, which does not add these gases.
keyPoints: Gases like carbon dioxide trap heat, and burning coal, oil and gas adds more of them.
A warmer Earth changes weather patterns, with heavier rain in some places and longer dry times in others.
Using power from the sun and wind can help slow these changes.
watch.contentNote: The video includes footage of extreme weather, such as storms, floods and drought. Preview it first. Learners can read the written summary instead, and no one should be asked about weather events they have lived through.

visual.description: A two-part diagram. On the left, a small card for one day at Sunrise School shows a rain cloud and the words 'Today: heavy rain'. It is labelled 'Weather'. On the right, a simple bar chart shows 12 months, with tall blue bars in the rainy-season months and short bars in the dry-season months. It is labelled 'Climate: average of 30 years'. Below, three small pictures show adaptations: a covered walkway, a drinking-water station and a ramp.
visual.alt: Diagram comparing one rainy day (weather) with a 30-year pattern of wet and dry months (climate), with pictures of a covered walkway, a water station and a ramp.

sensitiveNotes: Some learners may have lived through floods, storms or drought. Keep the lesson on patterns and preparation, don't ask learners about weather events they experienced, and let anyone step back from the discussion.
Preview the video first: it includes footage of extreme weather. The written summary covers the same ideas without the images.
educatorNotes: The video is about climate change, which goes a little beyond this lesson. Present it as an extension: climate can change slowly over many years.
You could replace the Mali, Yemen and Mongolia examples with a local one, such as how people in your area prepare for the rainy or hot season.

Rewrote simpler English at about grade 3; added season and monsoon to the glossary so every word appears in the text.
Moved the correct answers to first and second positions and evened out option lengths.
Rewrote the video summary from the video's narration, keeping it calm; moved the Base44 content warning into contentNote.
